blocks.x: A four-month research and development project, formulating and prototyping a bio-leather material using watermelon waste.

Watermelon, or Citrullus lanatus, is rich with proteins and amino acids, and the rind dry, fibrous, papery. Using a variety of methods for breaking down organic material, I recombined the watermelon with agar agar, glycerin, and sometimes natural pigment dyes, to create sheets and samples of usable “Watermelon Leather”.

Forging leather alternatives has surprisingly less to do with reducing slaughterhouse practices, and more to do with the damaging and toxic treatments carried out on the hides in post-processing. Beyond the chemical waste and pollution, it’s the amount of water needed for each individual hide.

blocks.x: The project was inspired by research robot studies, including Salto-1P. Investigating non-verbal gestural communication via exploration of a specific avenue of robot interaction became the clear direction for this study. The goal was to isolate non-verbal gestures of ear movements as they occur conversationally between animals.

This project aims to discover whether animalistic non-verbal gestural communication bears potential to be researched as an alternative Human-Robot Interaction. Conducted between August 2022 and December 2022, this project investigates whether there are familiar or universal kineme expressions between human and non-human entities.

blocks.x: The findings of this project prove conclusively that certain gestural expressions are universally recognized and understood as communicating an emotional state. 100% of participants conceded that animals are emotionally expressive beings. 90% of participants stated they felt a sense of emotional communication from the images once the questionnaire had been completed. Based on the data, the images had a success rate of 60% in conveying non-verbal communication. Additionally 86% of the images had their intended expression within those which scored highest, with 16% having been unrecognized by the participants.

Mandelbrot’s fractals; Gaetano Pesce’s Pratt Chair process

blocks.x: Two words were pulled blindly from a bowl: Chaos and Soap Dish. The goal of the project was to procure a specific emotional response through physical object by use of color, material, form, and narrative.

In my search for visual language which would inspire the design, I became drawn in two directions. Firstly, to Mandelbrot’s fractals, and their mathematically sporadic nature. Secondly, to Gaetano Pesce’s Pratt Chair process. By altering his mixture density with each chair, they became less and less structured, while still obeying certain constraints. I wanted to emulate his process, while straying between the boundary of his implementation of constraint, and my interpretation of chaos as being boundless.

x: Agar agar, latex, glycerin, natural pigments, shell and other natural inclusions

blocks.x: An open-ended search for new wearable materials that are skin-safe, sustainable and planet-positive.

Running in parallel with my digital work, these are agar agar based materials made with glycerin, natural pigments and sometimes other natural components: shells, fibres, latex. I look for the aqueous and the membranous, sliding scales of translucency, materials that most closely resemble something alive, and that hold real potential for integrating technology into what we wear.

about:
Hi, I’m Ariana, a multimedia industrial and graphic designer, design and design systems researcher, and Embodied AI specialist.

My work has become a hybrid between industrial product design and abstract emotional investigation. Coming from fine art and mixed media, I approach design by asking how it might shape an emotion, an experience, or a relationship: the emotion of a thing, the experience of a place, our relationship to the world.

At Drew University I explored mediums like oil and watercolor, acrylic, paper and mixed material assemblage, and ceramics, establishing material associations that would continue to guide how I make. At California College of the Arts I grew that into a cross-disciplinary practice, balancing an interplay between biomaterial whimsy, speculative world-building, CAD, CMF rendering, and rapid fabrication. My thesis, Learning Bodies, imagines biomimetic post-human anatomy, modular body modification, and bio-signaling technology inspired by deep-ocean creatures. It was nominated for the Steve Jobs Fellowship in 2024.

Today I work where bodies meet machines, in embodied AI, and every project still starts with the same questions: how does this feel, who is it for, and what can it teach us about being a body in the world?
